items.md: The paper asks how much the geographic proximity of a community college changes whether and where nearby students enroll, and whether they finish degrees. Miller (2025) uses five community college branch-campus openings in Texas between 1997 and 2012 (Table 1, p. 19). She compares high school graduates within 20 minutes driving time of a new campus with graduates 20–40 minutes away in the same commuting zone, before and after opening. The contribution has three parts. First, it offers plausibly causal evidence on college proximity, where earlier work was descriptive or used distance as an instrument (p. 4). Second, it studies two-year rather than four-year openings, where distance is more salient (p. 4). Third, linked student-level data let her separate extensive-margin entry from substitution across colleges. The paper does not study firms, industries or patents; every outcome is a student outcome.

items.md: **Data.** Education Research Center (University of Texas at Dallas) records on the universe of Texas public high school students, 1993 to 2020, matched to within-state public two-year and four-year enrollment and degrees. High school coordinates (NCES Common Core of Data) proxy for home address; college locations come from IPEDS plus state and association campus lists; driving times come from Open Route Service (p. 5).

q.exact: 3 Data I use administrative data from the Education Research Center (ERC) at the University of Texas at Dallas covering the universe of Texas public high school students from 1993 to 2020.

items.md: **Design.** A "ring method" generalized difference-in-differences. Treated students attend a high school within 20 minutes driving time of any opening college. Controls are 20–40 minutes away and in the same commuting zone. The five openings are pooled (p. 7); event time is trimmed to five years either side (p. 9).

items.md: **Identifying assumption.** Generalized parallel trends (conditional on covariates) and no anticipation (pp. 9–10). High school fixed effects absorb fixed residential sorting. Sorting in response to the opening is argued unlikely because it would require changing high schools (p. 10).

q.exact: The primary concern in the instrumental variable set- ting is residential sorting on unobservable factors that cannot be controlled for in the data.

$$Y_{it} = D_{it}\Gamma_{it}\theta + \phi_{s(i)} + \rho_{cz(i)t} + \beta_X X_{it} + \epsilon_{ist}$$
where $Y_{it}$ is the outcome, $D_{it}$ the treatment indicator, $\phi_{s(i)}$ high school fixed effects, $\rho_{cz(i)t}$ commuting-zone-by-year fixed effects, $X_{it}$ individual covariates (race, ethnicity, gender, economic disadvantage, standardized math and English language arts scores), and $\epsilon_{ist}$ the error (Eq. 1, p. 8). $\Gamma$ and $\theta$ are not defined beyond the treatment-effect parameterization. Untreated observations alone estimate the fixed effects (Eq. 2), giving $\hat{Y}_{it}(0)$ and $\hat{\tau}_{it}=Y_{it}-\hat{Y}_{it}(0)$ (Eqs. 3–4), averaged by years since opening (p. 9).
**Inference.** Standard errors clustered at the high school; 95% confidence intervals (pp. 8, 22). Pre-trends use the robust Borusyak, Jaravel, & Spiess test on untreated observations only (p. 9).

items.md: **Threats.** Colleges may be sited where local demand is growing; the paper relies on pre-trends and the narrow 20 versus 40 minute contrast (pp. 10–11). Spillover into the control ring is not formally examined.

q.exact: In this paper, I overcome this chal- lenge by using plausibly exogenous variation in college choice sets from community college openings in a difference in difference framework, comparing the educational outcomes of students who graduated from high school just before versus just after the college opens.

items.md: The setting is Texas. The primary sample is graduates of Texas public high schools between 1996 and 2020 with valid tenth-grade standardized test scores, standardized within cohort (p. 5). The five openings are Tarrant County SE (1997), Alamo NW Vista (1999), Lone Star Cy-Fair (2003), Tarrant County Trinity River (2010) and Lone Star University Park (2012) (Table 1, p. 19). All were branch campuses of existing community college systems, in or near large metropolitan areas (Fort Worth, San Antonio, Houston), not satellite campuses with limited offerings (p. 6). Other openings, such as Austin Community College, were excluded because they lack separate enrollment records (footnote 2, p. 6). Figure 2 counts 163 non-opening two-year colleges, 38 private four-year and 37 public four-year institutions (p. 20). Treated students would save about 10 minutes driving time (one-way) by attending the new college instead of their next-closest option (p. 7). Enrollment is measured within one year of high school graduation (footnote 5, p. 13). The number of students and school-year observations is not reported in this version.

items.md: The causal claim for the first stage and substitution is fairly credible. The ring contrast is tight (20 versus 40 minutes, same commuting zone), high school fixed effects remove fixed siting and sorting, and the imputation estimator handles staggered timing. The author is candid that the pre-trend evidence is imperfect: small, marginally significant pre-period increases appear for any-college and two-year enrollment (pp. 11–12). The dump does not show the plots, so I cannot judge how small "quantitatively small" is against post-period effects of only about 1 to 3 percentage points.

The main inference concern is that treatment varies across only five openings, yet standard errors are clustered at the high school (p. 8). Shocks common to all schools around one campus are not absorbed by high-school clustering, so confidence intervals may be too narrow. This is my judgment; the draft does not discuss it. A second concern is spillovers. Figure 3 shows enrollment falling "quickly" past 20 minutes, not to zero, so the 20–40 minute controls may be partly treated, which would bias effects toward zero. Third, the degree outcomes are weaker causal claims: earlier cohorts are redefined as treated through transfer or delayed entry (p. 13), so the pre-period is not a clean placebo, and the associate's result is a roughly 1 percentage point change off a roughly six percent base. The paper calls its enrollment findings "suggestive" and the draft is preliminary, with robustness to alternative treatment definitions listed as future work (p. 15).
External validity is narrow by the author's own account: dense metros with many existing colleges, and an average time saving of about 10 minutes (pp. 7, 14).

Transfer to a project on community or technical college openings and local firms, industry mix and innovation: the design transfers in structure (event study around openings, imputation estimator, geographic rings) but not in outcomes, since Miller measures students, not establishments or patents. Firm-side analysis would need geocoded establishment or inventor data, and the 20-minute student catchment may be too small for firm effects that operate through commuting zones, so the control ring could be contaminated. The weak first stage in dense metros (about 1 percentage point extensive-margin entry) suggests human-capital supply shocks, and so firm effects, would be small for similar openings; rural or "education desert" openings are where larger effects are more plausible (p. 15).

Robustness to alternative treatment definitions, heterogeneity by student characteristics such as race-ethnicity, and more outcomes such as college quality and major choice (stated by the author, p. 15).
Openings in rural areas or "education deserts" 30 minutes or more from the nearest community college, which this sample does not cover (p. 15).
Not addressed in this version: labor-market, firm, industry or innovation outcomes, and formal tests for spillover into the control ring.

For education policy, the results suggest that a nearby new community college mostly redistributes students among existing colleges, while still raising associate's completion by about 1 percentage point without lowering bachelor's completion (pp. 13–14). Openings, closings and mergers in dense metros may therefore matter more for persistence than for access. For future research on local economic effects, the paper provides a template for staggered openings with distance rings and a clear decomposition into first stage, extensive margin and substitution, plus a reminder that the first stage must be established before attributing downstream effects to an opening. Firm and innovation studies should check whether new campuses actually add students and graduates locally, or only reshuffle them, before expecting local economic changes. Extensions to rural settings are the natural next step (p. 15).
